# What you just built

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Run a talker on an emulated board](run-a-talker.md)

In this chapter you open the two packages chapter 1 scaffolded and ask
`nros` what it built from them. At the end you can say which file holds the
talker's code, which file chose the board and the middleware, and what an
*image* is: the one program `nros run` built and booted. You change nothing
yet; every step reads.

Run the steps from the root of `sensor_ws`, where chapter 1 left you.

## List the packages

```bash probe=210 track=installed variant=qemu
nros list
```

`nros list` prints each package of the workspace with its kind and its
directory. For a Rust project:

```text
ws list (/home/you/sensor_ws):
  rust       sensor_node               src/sensor_node
  other      sensor_node_bringup       src/sensor_node_bringup
ws list: 0 msg, 1 rust consumer
```

A C or C++ project lists `sensor_node` as a CMake package instead. The
bringup's kind is `other` in every language: it holds no code to compile.

Two packages, two roles. Everything you add to this project in the later
chapters is another package with one of these roles, or a few more lines in
the bringup. The shape of the workspace never changes; it only gains
packages. If you come from ROS 2, both roles are familiar:

| Your workspace | Role | In ROS 2 terms |
|---|---|---|
| `src/sensor_node/` | **node package** | a package holding one composable node (`rclcpp_components`) |
| `src/sensor_node_bringup/` | **bringup package** | a `<pkg>_bringup` package: configuration and launch, no code |

## Read the node package

A node package is one node, built as a library. It has no `main()` and names
no board and no middleware. Its files, in the language you picked:

<!-- tabs -->

#### Rust

```text
src/sensor_node/
├── Cargo.toml          # a library crate and its dependencies
├── package.xml         # the ROS 2 manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/lib.rs          # the talker
```

`src/lib.rs` declares the node in two parts. `register` runs once at startup
and states what the node creates: one publisher on `/chatter` and one timer
that fires every 1,000 ms. `on_callback` is what runs each time the timer
fires:

```rust
fn register(ctx: &mut NodeContext<'_>) -> NodeResult<()> {
    let mut node = ctx.create_node(NodeOptions::new("sensor_node"))?;
    let pub_chatter = node.create_publisher_for_topic::<StringMsg>("/chatter")?;
    let _timer =
        node.create_timer_for_callback_name("on_tick", TimerDuration::from_millis(1000))?;
    node.callback_for_name("on_tick")
        .publishes_entity(&pub_chatter)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

The file's last line, `nros::node!(Talker);`, exports the node so a program
can run it. `Cargo.toml` names the class the package exports,
`sensor_node::Talker`, and lists `nros` as a dependency with
`version = "*"`. Nothing of nano-ros comes from crates.io: the build points
that dependency at the nano-ros your `nros` installed.

#### C

```text
src/sensor_node/
├── CMakeLists.txt      # the library and the class it registers
├── nros-codegen.toml   # the largest string the node's messages carry
├── package.xml         # the ROS 2 manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/Talker.c        # the talker
```

`src/Talker.c` is a state struct, a timer callback and a `configure`
function. `configure` runs once at startup, on a node and an executor the
program hands it, and creates one publisher on `/chatter` and one timer that
fires every second. The file's last line exports the pair:

```c
RCLC_C_COMPONENT(talker_t, talker_configure)
```

`CMakeLists.txt` registers the class the bringup names:

```cmake
nano_ros_add_node(sensor_node CLASS sensor_node::Talker TYPED
    SOURCES src/Talker.c
    DEPLOY  linux)
```

`DEPLOY linux` also builds the node as a stand-alone program on your host,
for testing it alone. It does not choose the board the project builds for;
the bringup does that.

#### C++

```text
src/sensor_node/
├── CMakeLists.txt                  # the library and the class it registers
├── include/sensor_node/Talker.hpp  # the Talker class
├── nros-codegen.toml               # the largest string the node's messages carry
├── package.xml                     # the ROS 2 manifest: <depend>std_msgs</depend>
└── src/Talker.cpp                  # its two members
```

The node is a class with a `configure(rclcpp::Node&)` member, the shape of a
composable node. `configure` runs once at startup, creates one publisher on
`/chatter`, and binds `on_tick` as a timer that fires every second:

```cpp
class Talker {
    ::rclcpp::Publisher<std_msgs::msg::String> pub_;
    ::rclcpp::Timer timer_;
    int count_ = 0;

    void on_tick();

  public:
    ::rclcpp::Result configure(::rclcpp::Node& node);
};
```

`CMakeLists.txt` registers the class the bringup names:

```cmake
nano_ros_add_node(sensor_node CLASS sensor_node::Talker
    SOURCES src/Talker.cpp
    DEPLOY  linux)
```

`DEPLOY linux` also builds the node as a stand-alone program on your host,
for testing it alone. It does not choose the board the project builds for;
the bringup does that.

<!-- /tabs -->

In every language, `package.xml` is a standard ROS 2 manifest, and its
`<depend>std_msgs</depend>` line is the only place the message package is
named. The build generates the `std_msgs` code from your ROS 2 install, which
is why chapter 1 sourced ROS 2 before the first run. You never write message
code by hand, and you never commit it.

The same node package builds for any board, because nothing in it says
`mps2-an385`, `zenoh` or `serial`. Those words belong to the bringup.

## Read the bringup

```bash probe=220 track=installed variant=qemu
cat src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml
```

Comments trimmed, a Rust project's file is:

```toml
[system]
name = "sensor_node"
rmw = "zenoh"
ros_edition = "humble"
domain_id = 0

[[component]]
pkg = "sensor_node"
class = "sensor_node::Talker"
name = "sensor_node"

[image.baremetal]
board = "mps2-an385-baremetal"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"
```

A C or C++ project's file differs only in the `class` line's spelling, which
is the class the package registers. The bringup holds `package.xml` and this
`system.toml`, and no code. Its three tables answer three questions:

- **`[system]`: how the nodes reach ROS 2.** `rmw` is the middleware, the
  `--rmw zenoh` you passed to `nros setup`. `ros_edition` is the ROS 2
  release your peers run, and `domain_id` is the ROS 2 domain.
- **`[[component]]`: which nodes run.** One row per node: the package, the
  class it registers, and the node's name at run time. Chapter 3 adds a
  second row.
- **`[image.baremetal]`: what program is built, for which board.** The
  `board` line chose the MPS2-AN385 with no operating system. The `locator`
  line says how the program reaches its zenoh router: over the board's first
  serial port, UART 0, at 115,200 baud.

Every configuration choice of the project lives in this file, never in a
node package. Moving the talker to another board is another `[image.*]`
table; switching the middleware is the `rmw` line. Neither touches
`src/sensor_node/`.

## Ask what `nros run` runs

`nros run sensor_node` worked in chapter 1, but you never said which board.
Ask `nros` how it decided, without building or booting anything:

```bash probe=230 track=installed variant=qemu
nros run sensor_node --dry-run --why
```

`--dry-run` prints the run plan instead of carrying it out, and `--why` adds
where each part of the plan came from. The parts that matter here (a real
run, trimmed):

```text
image = "sensor_node_bringup:baremetal"
verb = "run"

[runner]
package = "nros_runner_qemu"
name = "qemu"

[target]
emulator = "qemu:mps2-an385"

[console]
kind = "semihosting"

[link]
kind = "serial"
locator = "serial/UART_0#baudrate=115200"
rmw = "zenoh"

[provenance]
image = "rung 3, `<node>`: `sensor_node` is the only component of `sensor_node_bringup`, whose only image this is"
link = "image"
"target.emulator" = "board"
```

Read it from the top:

- **`image`** is `sensor_node_bringup:baremetal`: the bringup, a colon, and
  the name of its `[image.baremetal]` table. That is the full name of what
  you ran.
- **`[provenance] image`** explains the shortcut. You typed the name of a
  node; `sensor_node` is the only node of `sensor_node_bringup`, and that
  bringup has only one image, so the name picked exactly one image.
- **`[target]`** and **`[runner]`** say the image runs in QEMU's
  MPS2-AN385, booted by the `qemu` runner. Their provenance is `board`: the
  board's own description states how it runs, so the bringup does not.
- **`[link]`** is the `locator` line of the image, and it is why `nros run`
  started a zenoh router on a serial device. **`[console]`** says the
  program's printed output comes through QEMU's semihosting, apart from the
  serial port the messages use.

## See what the build left behind

Chapter 1's run left more in the workspace than the two packages:

```bash probe=240 track=installed variant=qemu
ls
```

```text
build  generated  nros-sdk.lock  src
```

- **`src/`** holds the two packages, and nothing else. It is the only
  directory you write in.
- **`generated/`** holds the message code the build generated from your ROS 2
  install: `std_msgs`, and `builtin_interfaces`, which `std_msgs` depends on.
  Adding a `<depend>` to a node's `package.xml` adds a directory here on the
  next build. Chapter 5 adds your own message package and finds its code here
  too.
- **`build/`** holds the image's build tree, the program's generated
  `main()`, and each run's logs. The board's console from chapter 1 is in
  `build/nros/run/sensor_node_bringup_baremetal/console.log`, which is the
  first file to read when a run goes wrong.
- **`nros-sdk.lock`** records what the build was made from: the versions of
  the ROS 2 message packages it generated code from, and the source of the
  zenoh client it compiled. The scaffold's `.gitignore` leaves it in, so it
  is committed with your sources and a teammate's build uses the same inputs.

The scaffold's `.gitignore` leaves out `build/` and `generated/`. You can
delete both at any time: the next `nros run` makes them again, which takes as
long as chapter 1's first run did.

## What just happened

You met the three nano-ros ideas every later chapter builds on.

**A node package is code that runs anywhere.** It is a library holding one
node. It has no `main()` and names no board, no middleware and no ROS 2
release, so the same package goes into an image for this emulated board, an
image for your Linux host, or an image for a board with an RTOS, without a
second copy.

**A bringup package says what runs where.** It holds no code: only
`system.toml`, which lists the nodes (`[[component]]`), how they reach ROS 2
(`[system]`), and the programs to build (`[image.*]`). Where a ROS 2 project
spreads that across launch files, parameter files and environment variables,
nano-ros keeps it in one file, because on a microcontroller it must be known
when the program is built: there is no shell, file system or environment to
read it from at run time.

**An image is one program for one board.** Each `[image.*]` table is one
image: the bringup's nodes, built with one middleware for one board, into one
file you can boot or flash. `nros run` built `sensor_node_bringup:baremetal`
in chapter 1 and booted it in QEMU. Nothing in `src/` contains that program's
`main()`: `nros` generated it under `build/` from the image table, together
with the generated message code and the build settings the board needs.

This is where nano-ros differs most from a ROS 2 workspace. In ROS 2, a
package builds executables, and you start each one with `ros2 run` or a
launch file, as its own process, on a machine that already runs an operating
system. In nano-ros there is no separate step that starts nodes: the image
*is* the whole system for its board. Every node of the bringup is compiled
into it, they share one executor, and booting the image starts all of them.
Running two images means two programs, on one board each. A bare-metal board
has no processes at all, so one program per board is the only shape that fits
it, and nano-ros uses the same shape on every board, Linux included, so a
project does not change shape when it changes board.

Everything under `src/` is yours to edit and commit. Everything under
`build/` is derived from `src/` and your ROS 2 install, so none of it is
committed and none of it is edited; the scaffold's `.gitignore` already
leaves it out. [How a build becomes an image](../background/how-a-build-becomes-an-image.md)
explains the layers inside an image and why the program is generated rather
than written.

## Design background

The two roles and the generated program follow
[RFC-0121](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0121-workspace-first-project-layout.md)
D1 to D3. The run plan `--dry-run` prints is
[RFC-0118](https://github.com/NEWSLabNTU/nano-ros/blob/main/docs/design/0118-target-execution-model.md)'s.
